label: Steps a day
body:
Heart and longevity benefits climb
steeply up to about 8,000 steps.
No gym needed. A 10-min walk after
meals also blunts sugar spikes.
caption:
You don't need 10,000 steps. But you probably need more than you're doing.

The 10k number came from a 1960s pedometer ad — not science.

What large studies actually show: the risk of early death drops steeply as daily steps rise, and the benefit starts levelling off around 7,000–8,000 steps for most adults.

Easy ways to get there:
→ 10-minute walk after each meal
→ Take calls standing or walking
→ Stairs instead of the lift
→ Park or get off one stop early

Walking is the most underrated health habit there is.

→ 15–20 min of midday sun on arms and legs, a few times a week

→ Sugar hits your blood fast
→ You're hungry again soon
→ It's easy to drink 3 oranges' worth in 30 seconds

→ Better blood sugar control

Rest days

Training hard every single day and not seeing results? You might need less, not more.

→ Poor sleep and low energy
→ Higher injury risk

The rule of thumb: about 48 hours before training the same muscle group hard again. Walking and stretching on rest days is great.

Your resting

Your resting heart rate is one of the simplest health signals you can track — and it's free.

→ 60–100 bpm is the normal adult range
→ Regular exercise usually brings it lower over time
→ A rise of several beats for days can mean poor sleep, stress, dehydration or an oncoming illness

Track it for a week to learn your baseline. Changes matter more than one reading.

label: Healthy blood pressure
body:
Below 120/80 mmHg is ideal.
140/90 or above on repeat checks
is high BP. It rarely has symptoms,
so the only way to know is to check.
caption:
High blood pressure is called the silent killer for a reason. Most people with it feel completely fine.

Until a heart attack or stroke.

What the numbers mean:
→ Below 120/80 — ideal
→ 120–139 / 80–89 — higher than ideal, time to act
→ 140/90 or above on repeat readings — high blood pressure

What brings it down:
→ Less salt (pickles, papad, namkeen, packaged food)
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Losing even a few kg if you're overweight
→ Less alcohol, no smoking

Every adult should know their number. Get it checked at least once a year.

Breathe out
the stress

Feeling wound up before a meeting, an exam or a tough conversation? Your breath is the fastest off-switch you have.

When you breathe out slowly, your heart rate drops a little and your body shifts out of "fight or flight".

→ Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts
→ Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6 counts
→ Keep your shoulders relaxed
→ Repeat for 5 minutes

Weight change comes from your total calories over days and weeks — not the time on the clock.

→ Late-night snacking is usually extra food, not a meal
→ It's often chips, sweets and biscuits
→ A heavy dinner right before bed can cause acidity and poor sleep
→ Poor sleep makes you hungrier the next day

The smart move: eat dinner 2–3 hours before bed and keep it balanced. If you're truly hungry later, curd, fruit or a handful of nuts.

→ Chai and coffee (2 tsp a cup adds up fast)

Multigrain means

body: Many multigrain breads and biscuits are mostly maida with a sprinkle of other grains. Check the ingredients list — the first item is the main one.
caption:
"Multigrain" on the pack sounds healthy. But it doesn't mean whole grain.

It just means more than one grain is in there — even if it's a tiny amount.

Many multigrain breads, biscuits and atta blends are mostly refined flour (maida) with a little oats, ragi or flax added for the label.

How to check in 10 seconds:
→ Read the ingredients list — they're listed from most to least
→ First ingredient should be "whole wheat" or another whole grain
→ "Wheat flour" or "refined wheat flour" usually means maida
→ Compare fibre: aim for 6 g or more per 100 g

Trust the ingredients, not the front of the pack.

label: Did you know

Your ears clean
themselves.
body: Ear wax moves out on its own as you chew and talk. Cotton buds push it deeper and can hurt your eardrum. Just wipe the outer ear.
caption:
Cleaning your ears with cotton buds every day? You're probably doing more harm than good.

Ear wax isn't dirt. It traps dust, keeps the ear canal moist and helps fight infection.

Your ears are self-cleaning: jaw movement slowly pushes old wax outwards.

What cotton buds actually do:
→ Push wax deeper, causing blockages
→ Scratch the delicate skin of the ear canal
→ Can damage your eardrum

What to do instead:
→ Wipe the outer ear with a cloth after a bath
→ Never put hairpins, keys or oil drops inside
→ See a doctor for pain, blocked hearing or discharge

Leave your ears alone. They've got this.

label: HbA1c warning line
body:
HbA1c shows your average sugar
over the last 2–3 months.
Below 5.7% normal. 5.7–6.4%
prediabetes. 6.5%+ diabetes.
caption:
A fasting sugar test shows one morning. HbA1c shows the last 2–3 months.

That's why doctors trust it.

HbA1c measures how much sugar has stuck to your red blood cells, which live about 3 months.

What the result means:
→ Below 5.7% — normal
→ 5.7% to 6.4% — prediabetes
→ 6.5% or higher — diabetes (confirmed by your doctor)

Prediabetes is the window where lifestyle changes work best:
→ Lose 5–7% of your body weight if overweight
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Fewer refined carbs and sugary drinks

Over 30, or diabetes in the family? Ask for an HbA1c test.

sections.text: Pressure, squeezing or pain lasting minutes.

sections.title: Spreading
sections.text: To the arm, jaw, neck or back.

sections.title: With
sections.text: Breathlessness, cold sweat, nausea.

caption:
Knowing these signs can save a life — maybe someone at home.

In a heart attack, every minute matters.

Common warning signs:
→ Chest pressure, squeezing or pain that lasts more than a few minutes
→ Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, back or upper stomach
→ Shortness of breath
→ Cold sweat, nausea or light-headedness

Women, older people and people with diabetes often have milder or unusual symptoms — like only breathlessness, tiredness or "gas".

What to do:
→ Call 108 or 112 straight away
→ Don't drive yourself to hospital
→ Don't wait to "see if it passes"

Your waist size may say more about your health than your weight does.

→ Poor sleep, weight gain and low mood

→ Have alcohol-free days every week

Can't sleep?
Get up.

Tossing and turning for an hour? Staying in bed is making it worse.

When you lie awake night after night, your brain starts linking your bed with frustration, not sleep.

Sleep doctors use a simple rule:
→ If you're awake for about 20 minutes, get out of bed
→ Sit somewhere dim and quiet
→ Read a paper book or listen to something calm — no phone
→ Go back to bed only when you feel sleepy
→ Repeat if needed

caption:
Wearing a sweat suit or working out in a hot room to "melt the fat"? It doesn't work like that.

Sweat is water your body releases to cool down.

How much you sweat depends on heat, humidity, genetics and fitness — not on how much fat you're burning.

What really happens:
→ You lose water weight
→ The scale drops for a few hours
→ You drink water, and it comes right back
→ Too much sweating can leave you dehydrated and dizzy

What does burn fat: a consistent calorie deficit, strength training, daily movement and enough protein.

label: BMI cutoff for Indians

counts as overweight, 25+ as obese.
The global cutoffs (25/30) miss

caption:
Your BMI says "normal"? For Indians, the usual chart can be misleading.

Asian Indians tend to develop diabetes and heart disease at lower body weights than Western populations.

That's why Indian guidelines use lower cutoffs:
→ 18.5–22.9 — normal
→ 23–24.9 — overweight
→ 25 and above — obese

You can't go from scrolling and stressing straight to deep sleep. Your brain needs a runway.

A wind-down routine is a set of calm steps you do in the same order every night. Over time, it becomes a signal to your brain that sleep is coming.

Try a 30-minute routine:
→ Dim the lights in your room
→ Phone on charge, away from the bed
→ Wash up and change
→ Read a few pages of a paper book
→ Light stretching or slow breathing

Keep it the same every night, including weekends.

Muscle soaks up

The more muscle you have — and the more you use it — the more sugar it can absorb.

→ Strength training improves insulin sensitivity
→ A walk after meals lowers sugar spikes
→ Sitting all day makes blood sugar control worse
→ Losing muscle with age raises diabetes risk

Two strength sessions a week plus daily walking is a powerful combination.

→ Doing too much too soon
→ Weak hips and thighs
→ Running through sharp pain
→ Carrying a lot of extra weight

→ Increase distance gradually

→ Mix running with walking at first

label: Fever starts here

A temperature of 38°C (100.4°F)
or higher counts as a fever.
Rest and fluids help. See a doctor
if it lasts 3 days or is very high.
caption:
Feeling warm? A thermometer settles it. Not every warm forehead is a fever.

Normal body temperature is around 37°C (98.6°F), and it changes a little through the day.

A fever is usually 38°C (100.4°F) or higher.

What helps at home:
→ Rest
→ Plenty of fluids — water, ORS, soups, coconut water
→ Light clothing and a cool room

See a doctor if:
→ Fever lasts more than 3 days
→ It's 39.4°C (103°F) or higher
→ There's a rash, severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or trouble breathing
→ It's an infant, older person, or someone with a long-term illness

During dengue season, don't ignore a fever.

Five short nights, then sleeping till noon on Sunday? That's not catching up — it's jet lag at home.

Extra sleep at the weekend can ease some tiredness. But it doesn't fully undo a week of short sleep.

→ Hard to fall asleep on Sunday night
→ Groggy Monday mornings
→ More cravings and lower mood

A better plan:
→ Keep weekend wake time within an hour of weekdays
→ Take a short afternoon nap if you need it
→ Fix weekday sleep, rather than repaying it later

No pain,

caption:
"No pain, no gain" sounds tough. It also causes a lot of injuries.

There's a big difference between effort and pain.

Normal (keep going):
→ Muscles burning near the end of a set
→ Heavy breathing during cardio
→ Mild soreness 1–2 days later

Warning signs (stop):
→ Sharp or stabbing pain
→ Pain in a joint, not a muscle
→ Pain that gets worse as you continue
→ Swelling, or pain that lasts more than a few days

Results come from training consistently for months — not from destroying yourself in one session.

Challenge yourself. Don't punish yourself.

The good news:
→ Missing a single day didn't derail the habit
→ Simple habits stuck faster than complex ones

How to make habits stick:
→ Start tiny (2 push-ups, not 50)
→ Tie it to something you already do ("after brushing, I…")
→ Same time, same place
→ Track it on a calendar

→ Acne and oily skin
→ Extra hair on the face or body

→ Losing 5–10% of body weight, if overweight
→ Strength training and daily walking
→ Protein and fibre in every meal, fewer refined carbs
→ Regular sleep

→ Water with meals is fine and can help you feel full

→ Eating slowly

→ Not lying down right after a big meal

Fatty liver is far more common than most people realise — and it usually has no symptoms.

→ People with a large waist or excess weight
→ People with diabetes or prediabetes
→ High triglycerides
→ Even "thin" people with belly fat

→ Losing 7–10% of body weight can reduce liver fat significantly
→ Daily activity
→ Cut sugary drinks, sweets and refined carbs
→ Avoid alcohol

"I can't lose weight because of my thyroid." Sometimes there's some truth to it — but usually less than people think.

Hypothyroidism (an underactive thyroid) slows metabolism and can cause modest weight gain, partly from fluid.

→ Tiredness and feeling cold

→ Unexplained weight gain

→ Get a TSH test
→ Take medicine exactly as prescribed
→ Then focus on food, movement and sleep

caption:
Indian summers are getting hotter. Knowing the signs of heatstroke can save a life.

Heat exhaustion comes first:
→ Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness
→ Headache, nausea, muscle cramps

Heatstroke is a medical emergency:
→ Body temperature 40°C (104°F) or higher
→ Confusion, slurred speech or fainting
→ Hot, dry skin — sweating may stop
→ Fast heartbeat

What to do:
→ Call 108 or 112
→ Move the person to shade or a cool room
→ Cool them fast: wet cloths, fan, cool water on skin
→ Give sips of water only if they're fully alert

Prevent it: avoid the sun from 12 to 4 PM, drink water often, and check on elderly neighbours.

→ Rest and fluids
→ Steam and warm salt-water gargles

label: Did you know
headline:
Your liver can
regrow.
body: The liver can regenerate after injury — even from a partial transplant. But long-term damage from alcohol or fatty liver leaves scars.
caption:
Your liver is the only organ that can regrow lost tissue. It's remarkable — but it has limits.

That's why living-donor liver transplants work: both the donor's and the recipient's liver pieces grow back towards full size.

Your liver handles over 500 jobs, including:
→ Filtering toxins and medicines
→ Storing energy
→ Making proteins that help blood clot
→ Processing fat

But repeated damage — from alcohol, fatty liver, or hepatitis — can cause scarring (cirrhosis) that doesn't heal.

→ Food and waste still in your gut
→ Hormones and the menstrual cycle
→ A hard workout (muscles hold water while they repair)

Your blood is constantly being renewed. Right now, your bone marrow is making millions of red blood cells every second.

Each red blood cell lives about 120 days, carrying oxygen around your body, before it's recycled.

→ Good sleep

caption:
Don't have time to exercise? You might have more than you think.

A large 2023 review of studies covering over 30 million people found that 75 minutes a week of moderate activity — about 11 minutes a day — was linked to a lower risk of early death, heart disease and some cancers.

→ A brisk walk to the market
→ Taking the stairs a few times a day
→ Cycling to a nearby friend's place
→ Dancing to three songs

That's the starting point, not the goal. The full benefit comes at 150 minutes a week.

→ Deep sleep — body repair, immune function, growth
→ REM sleep — dreaming, memory and emotions

Early in the night, cycles have more deep sleep. Later cycles have more REM.

What that means:
→ A full night gives you 4–6 cycles
→ Cutting sleep short from 7.5 to 5.5 hours mainly costs you REM
→ Waking at the end of a cycle often feels easier than waking in deep sleep

Loud snoring is often a family joke. Sometimes it's a sign of a serious sleep disorder.

→ Losing weight if overweight

→ Sleeping on your side

body: Cooking then cooling rice or potatoes turns some starch into resistant starch, which digests slowly and feeds gut bacteria. Refrigerate promptly.
caption:
Last night's rice may be gentler on your blood sugar than freshly cooked rice.

When starchy foods like rice, potatoes and pasta are cooked and then cooled, some of the starch changes structure. It becomes "resistant starch".

What resistant starch does:
→ Resists digestion, so it acts more like fibre
→ Feeds your good gut bacteria
→ Can lead to a smaller blood sugar rise

Reheating doesn't fully undo it.

Food safety matters with rice:
→ Cool cooked rice quickly and refrigerate within 1–2 hours
→ Eat it within a day
→ Reheat until steaming hot, only once

Cramps happen when the uterus contracts to shed its lining.

→ A hot water bag on the lower belly or back
→ Gentle movement: walking, stretching, yoga
→ Warm fluids and enough water
→ Rest and good sleep
→ Regular exercise through the month

→ Pain stops you from going to school, college or work
→ Painkillers don't help
→ Pain is getting worse over time
→ You have very heavy bleeding or pain during sex

Severe pain can be a sign of conditions like endometriosis, which is treatable.

Muscle turns

"If you stop going to the gym, all that muscle will turn to fat." It's a common belief — and biologically impossible.

→ Muscles shrink from less use
→ They burn fewer calories through activity
→ But often keep eating the same amount
→ So fat increases

That's why it looks like muscle "turned into" fat.

How to avoid it:
→ Keep some strength training, even once or twice a week
→ Adjust portions if you're less active
→ Stay active daily

Muscle is easier to keep than to build.

"Stop cracking your knuckles — you'll get arthritis!" Most of us were told this as kids.

That popping sound comes from a gas bubble forming in the fluid that cushions your joints when you stretch them.

Studies comparing habitual knuckle crackers with non-crackers found no higher rates of arthritis. One doctor even cracked the knuckles of only one hand for 60 years — and found no difference.

→ Pain when a joint cracks
→ Swelling or stiffness
→ Reduced movement
→ Cracking after an injury

caption:
Many Indian homes got a pulse oximeter during the pandemic. Here's how to read it properly.

SpO2 shows how much of your blood's haemoglobin is carrying oxygen.

What the numbers mean:
→ 95–100% — normal for most healthy people
→ 94% or below at rest — talk to a doctor
→ 92% or lower, or breathlessness at rest — seek urgent care

→ Sit and rest for a few minutes
→ Warm your hands first
→ Remove nail polish or artificial nails
→ Keep your hand still and at heart level
→ Wait for the number to settle

Keto promises rapid fat loss. But is it really better than other diets?

The ketogenic diet cuts carbs to very low levels — no rice, roti, fruit or dal in most versions.

What happens:
→ Fast weight loss in the first weeks — much of it water
→ Less appetite for some people
→ Hard to keep up with Indian meals and family food

Possible downsides:
→ Low fibre and constipation
→ Higher LDL cholesterol in some people
→ Missing out on fruit, pulses and whole grains

The best diet is one you can follow for years, not weeks.

→ Cook in fresh water until fully soft
→ Pressure cooking helps break them down further

→ Sprouting reduces gas-causing sugars even more
→ Add hing, jeera, ajwain or ginger while cooking
→ Increase pulses slowly so your gut adjusts

Dry, tired, burning eyes after a day of screens? It's called digital eye strain — and it's very common.

→ Every 20 minutes
→ Look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away
→ For 20 seconds

→ Blink deliberately and often
→ Keep your screen about an arm's length away, slightly below eye level
→ Match screen brightness to the room
→ Reduce glare from windows and overhead lights

→ Total food across the day
→ Protein and fibre in your meals
→ Not overeating later because you're starving

→ You have diabetes and your doctor recommends regular meals

Popping a painkiller for every headache, backache or period pain? Over-the-counter doesn't mean risk-free.

→ NSAIDs (like ibuprofen, diclofenac): stomach ulcers, acidity, kidney damage, raised BP

→ Never exceed the dose on the label
→ Check combination cold and flu medicines — they may contain the same drug
→ Take NSAIDs with food
→ Avoid them if you have kidney disease or stomach ulcers, unless a doctor says so

→ Protein and calcium-rich foods; check vitamin D
→ Regular sleep routine, cool bedroom

caption:
The low-fat craze of the 1990s taught us to fear all fat. It didn't make people healthier.

Eating fat doesn't directly turn into body fat. Weight gain happens when you eat more calories than you use — from any source.

→ Absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K
→ Hormones and brain health
→ Feeling satisfied after meals

→ Nuts and seeds
→ Fish
→ Mustard, groundnut and other vegetable oils in moderation
→ A little ghee

→ Trans fats (vanaspati, reused frying oil)
→ Lots of deep-fried snacks

→ Losing muscle from not using it
→ Bigger portions and more snacking
→ Less sleep and more stress

→ Extreme tiredness, restlessness or confusion

What to do:
→ Rest and drink plenty of fluids — ORS, water, soups
→ Avoid painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin unless a doctor advises
→ Prevent bites: no standing water, nets, full sleeves

caption:
Eat your carrots and you'll never need glasses? That's partly wartime propaganda.

During World War II, the British spread a story that their pilots' great night vision came from eating carrots — to hide the fact that they were using radar.

→ Carrots are rich in beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A
→ Vitamin A is essential for vision

caption:
Men, if you're getting up several times a night to pee, don't just blame age.

The prostate is a small gland below the bladder. As men age, it commonly enlarges, which can squeeze the urine tube.

→ Waking up at night to urinate, often
→ A weak or interrupted stream
→ Trouble starting
→ Feeling the bladder isn't empty
→ Urgency or dribbling

Most of the time it's benign prostatic enlargement, which is very treatable.

But see a doctor promptly if you have:
→ Blood in urine or semen
→ Pain while urinating
→ Bone pain or unexplained weight loss

→ At worry time, go through the list. Problem-solve what you can
→ When time's up, close the notebook

→ Bigger chunks reaching your stomach
→ Eating more before you feel full

"It's just stress, it's all in your head." Stress may start in the mind, but it shows up all over your body.

When stress is constant, your body stays in "fight or flight" mode for too long.

It can lead to:
→ Higher blood pressure and heart rate
→ Poor sleep
→ Headaches and muscle tension
→ Acidity, IBS flare-ups and appetite changes
→ More frequent infections
→ Higher blood sugar

Ways to lower stress that are backed by research:
→ Regular physical activity
→ Slow breathing — longer exhales
→ Good sleep
→ Talking to people you trust
→ Time in nature
→ Professional help when needed

Taking stress seriously is taking your health seriously.

The peel holds

Peeling your apples, cucumbers and potatoes? You might be throwing away some of the best parts.

→ Cucumbers

→ Chikoo and plums

→ Wash under running water and rub well

label: Sodium per gram salt
body:
Labels list sodium, not salt.
1 g of salt has about 400 mg sodium.
Multiply sodium by 2.5 for salt.
2,000 mg sodium = WHO's 5 g limit.
caption:
Food labels in India list "sodium", not salt. Here's how to read them.

Salt is sodium chloride. About 40% of salt is sodium.

The quick conversion:
→ 1 g of salt ≈ 400 mg of sodium
→ To get salt from sodium: multiply by 2.5
→ WHO's limit of 5 g salt ≈ 2,000 mg sodium a day

Examples:
→ Instant noodles with 1,000 mg sodium → 2.5 g salt — half your daily limit
→ A pack of chips with 500 mg sodium → 1.25 g salt
→ A pickle serving with 600 mg sodium → 1.5 g salt

Compare brands per 100 g and pick the lower one.

Your heart counts every milligram.

We use only 10%
of our brain?

caption:
"Humans only use 10% of their brains." It's a famous movie plot. It isn't true.

Brain scans show that over the course of a day, we use virtually every part of our brain. Even during sleep, many areas are active.

Different areas handle different tasks — movement, language, memory, emotions, vision — so not every part fires at the same moment.

And damage to almost any part of the brain causes noticeable problems — which wouldn't happen if 90% were unused.

What does help your brain work at its best:
→ Sleep
→ Physical activity
→ Learning new skills
→ Social connection
→ Managing blood pressure and blood sugar

You're already using all of it. Look after all of it.

Dal and rice

Your grandmother's dal-chawal was smarter than it looks.

Protein is made of building blocks called amino acids. Your body needs nine essential ones from food.

Plant proteins are usually low in one or two:
→ Grains (rice, wheat, millets) are low in lysine
→ Pulses (dal, rajma, chana) are low in methionine

Together, they fill each other's gaps — creating a more complete protein.

Classic Indian combos:
→ Dal and rice
→ Rajma-chawal
→ Chole with roti
→ Khichdi
→ Idli and dosa (rice + urad dal)
→ Besan roti

You don't need to combine them in the same meal — over the day works too. Add curd or paneer to boost protein further.

Stand up quickly and the room spins for a moment? That's a brief drop in blood pressure as blood pools in your legs.

It's common and usually harmless — especially if you:
→ Haven't had enough water
→ Stood up very fast
→ Have been ill, fasting or in the heat
→ Take some BP medicines

→ Sit up first, wait a few seconds, then stand
→ Drink enough fluids through the day
→ Flex your calf muscles before standing
→ Avoid standing still for long periods in heat

See a doctor if you:
→ Faint, or nearly faint
→ Feel dizzy often
→ Have chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness
→ Are older and falling

→ Gestational diabetes
→ High blood pressure
→ A difficult delivery

→ Protein: dal, paneer, eggs, curd, fish

Sore means it

caption:
Not sore after your workout? It doesn't mean it didn't work.

Muscle soreness (DOMS) usually happens when you:
→ Try a new exercise
→ Increase intensity or volume sharply
→ Do a lot of lowering movements, like downhill running

As your body adapts, you get less sore — even while you keep getting stronger.

Better signs of a good training plan:
→ You're gradually lifting more weight or doing more reps
→ Daily tasks feel easier
→ You recover well between sessions
→ You're sleeping well and feel energetic

Chasing soreness can lead to overtraining and injury.

Judge your progress by strength, not soreness.

Waking up with a stiff, aching back? How you sleep might be part of the problem.

Best positions for back comfort:
→ Side sleepers: bend your knees slightly and put a pillow between them, to keep your hips and spine aligned
→ Back sleepers: place a pillow under your knees to ease pressure on your lower back

→ A medium-firm mattress suits most people with back pain
→ Pillow height should keep your neck in line with your spine
→ Get out of bed by rolling to your side and pushing up with your arms

→ Build up to 10-second holds over weeks

→ Don't hold your breath or squeeze your stomach, thighs or buttocks
→ Don't practise while actually passing urine

caption:
Drinking three protein shakes a day for bigger gains? Your muscles can only use so much.

A large review of studies found that, for people doing strength training, muscle gains level off at around 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight per day.

→ Doesn't add much more muscle
→ Adds calories
→ Can cost a lot if it comes from supplements

What builds muscle:
→ Progressive strength training — lifting a little more over time
→ Enough protein, spread across meals
→ Enough total calories
→ Sleep and recovery
→ Consistency over months

Protein is a tool, not magic. Training does the building.

→ Plant your feet and feel the floor
→ Don't fight it — let it rise and fall

Afterwards:
→ Rest and drink water
→ Note what was happening before

Swallowed gum

"If you swallow chewing gum, it'll stay in your stomach for seven years!" Most of us heard this as children.

Rarely, swallowing large amounts of gum often — especially in young children, or along with coins or other objects — can cause a blockage.

→ Swallowing a piece by accident is fine

→ Teach young kids to spit gum out

caption:
Woke up feeling great, then saw a "poor sleep score" and felt tired all day? Your tracker might be wrong.

Smartwatches and rings estimate sleep using movement and heart rate. They're reasonably good at estimating total sleep time, but much less accurate at telling light, deep and REM sleep apart.

Some people become so anxious about their scores that their sleep gets worse — sleep researchers have even named this "orthosomnia".

How to use a tracker sensibly:
→ Look at weekly trends, not single nights
→ Notice patterns: late caffeine, alcohol, screens
→ Trust how you feel during the day

Signs of good sleep: falling asleep fairly easily, waking up refreshed, and staying alert during the day.

The best sleep tracker is how you feel.

Indian summers can be brutal for workouts. Training in high heat raises the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke.

caption:
"It's just a vitamin — it can't hurt." More isn't always better.

Some vitamins and minerals can build up in the body and become harmful in high doses.

Examples:
→ Vitamin D: very high doses over time can raise blood calcium, causing nausea, kidney problems and confusion
→ Vitamin A: excess can harm the liver and bones, and cause birth defects in pregnancy
→ Iron: too much can damage organs — and accidental overdose is dangerous for children
→ Vitamin B6: very high doses over time can damage nerves

Safe supplement use:
→ Test before you take — especially for vitamin D, B12 and iron
→ Follow the dose your doctor recommends
→ Check labels — many products combine the same vitamins
→ Keep supplements out of children's reach

Food first. Supplements when needed.

label: Reality check
headline:
Water with meals
ruins digestion?
body: Drinking water with meals doesn't dilute stomach acid enough to matter. It can help you feel full and digest food. Sip as you like.
caption:
"Don't drink water while eating — it dilutes your digestive juices." This is widely believed. It isn't supported by evidence.

Your stomach adjusts acid production to what you eat, and water passes through the stomach quickly.

Drinking water with meals:
→ Doesn't meaningfully weaken digestion
→ Can help soften food and move it along
→ Can help you feel fuller and eat a little less
→ Helps fibre do its job

Where moderation helps:
→ Gulping huge amounts during a meal can make you feel uncomfortably full
→ Some people with reflux feel better sipping rather than drinking large amounts

Drink water before, during or after meals — whatever feels comfortable.

label: Women's health
headline:
Bone health
for women
body: Bone loss speeds up after menopause. Strength training, calcium, vitamin D and protein help. Ask about a bone scan.
caption:
Osteoporosis — weak, brittle bones — is much more common in women than in men. Many find out only after a fracture.

Women have smaller bones to begin with, and bone loss speeds up after menopause as oestrogen falls.

Build strong bones early:
→ Strength training and impact exercise (walking, skipping, dancing)
→ Calcium-rich foods: milk, curd, paneer, ragi, til
→ Vitamin D: safe sun exposure and testing
→ Enough protein

Keep them strong later:
→ Keep up strength and balance training
→ Avoid smoking and limit alcohol
→ Prevent falls at home

Talk to your doctor about a bone density (DEXA) scan, especially after menopause, or earlier if you have risk factors like early menopause or long-term steroid use.

label: Did you know
headline:
Salt water soothes
a sore throat.
body: Gargling warm salt water can ease throat pain and loosen mucus. Half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, a few times a day.
caption:
Grandma's remedy for a sore throat has some science behind it.

Gargling with warm salt water can:
→ Ease throat pain and irritation
→ Loosen mucus
→ Help keep the throat clean

How to do it:
→ Mix about half a teaspoon of salt into a glass of warm (not hot) water
→ Gargle for 15–30 seconds, then spit it out
→ Repeat a few times a day

It's not a cure — most sore throats are caused by viruses and get better on their own in about a week.

Also helpful:
→ Warm fluids like soups and herbal tea
→ Honey (not for children under 1)
→ Rest

See a doctor for high fever, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or a sore throat lasting more than a week.

label: Minutes to offset sitting
body:
A large study found 60–75 min of
moderate activity a day may offset
the extra risk of sitting 8+ hours.
Desk job? Move more.
caption:
Sitting for 8+ hours a day at a desk? Here's how much movement it may take to balance it out.

A large analysis of over 1 million people, published in The Lancet, found that people who sat for long hours had a higher risk of early death.

But those who did about 60–75 minutes of moderate activity a day — like brisk walking or cycling — appeared to cancel out that extra risk.

That's more than the minimum 150 minutes a week. But it doesn't have to happen all at once:
→ 20-minute brisk walk in the morning
→ 10-minute walks after lunch and dinner
→ Taking stairs and walking during calls
→ An evening workout or game

And stand up every 30 minutes.

Desk jobs need active days.

label: Wellbeing
headline:
The morning
walk habit
body: A 20–30 minute walk soon after waking brings daylight for your body clock, movement for your heart, and quiet time for your mind.
caption:
If you could add just one habit this year, make it a morning walk.

In one simple routine, you get:
→ Daylight — which helps set your body clock and improves sleep at night
→ Movement — good for your heart, blood sugar and joints
→ Fresh air and quiet thinking time
→ A calmer start to the day

How to make it stick:
→ Lay out your shoes and clothes the night before
→ Start with 15 minutes and build to 30
→ Walk with a friend, neighbour or family member
→ Leave the phone in your pocket — or use it only for music
→ Pick a route with trees or a park if you can

On bad-air days, walk indoors or wait until the air clears.

Small steps every morning add up to a healthier year.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Walking isn't
real exercise?
body: Brisk walking counts as moderate activity and cuts the risk of heart disease, diabetes and depression. It's the most underrated workout there is.
caption:
"Walking doesn't count — you need to sweat in a gym." Many people believe this. The research disagrees.

Brisk walking — around 100 steps a minute, where you can talk but not sing — counts as moderate-intensity exercise.

Regular walking is linked to:
→ Lower risk of heart disease and stroke
→ Better blood sugar control and lower diabetes risk
→ Healthier weight
→ Better mood and less depression
→ Stronger bones and better sleep

And it's free, low-injury, and easy to fit into everyday life.

Make your walks count:
→ Walk briskly, not a stroll
→ 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week
→ Add hills or stairs for a challenge
→ Pair with 2 days of strength training

Never underestimate a walk.

label: Dinner before bed
body:
Finishing dinner 2–3 hours before
bed eases acidity and can improve
sleep. Late, heavy meals keep your
gut busy when it should rest.
caption:
Eating dinner at 10:30 PM and going to bed at 11? Your gut and your sleep may both be struggling.

Finishing your last big meal about 2–3 hours before bed can help:
→ Reduce acidity and heartburn
→ Improve sleep quality
→ Avoid that heavy, uncomfortable feeling at night

What happens with late, heavy meals:
→ Lying down soon after eating makes acid reflux more likely
→ Digestion can disturb sleep
→ Late meals are often bigger and less planned

Tips:
→ Shift dinner a little earlier, step by step
→ Make dinner lighter than lunch
→ If you're hungry late, have something small — curd, fruit or warm milk

Earlier, lighter dinners — better nights.

Small habits

body: A 10-minute walk, one less spoon of sugar, an earlier bedtime — tiny changes repeated for a year add up to real, lasting results.
caption:
This is post number 365. If you've been following along, thank you. Here's the most important lesson of the year.

Small habits seem too small to matter. But repeated every day, they compound.

What a year of small habits can look like:
→ A 10-minute walk after dinner → over 60 hours of walking
→ One less spoon of sugar in chai → more than 1 kg less sugar
→ 15 minutes earlier to bed → over 90 extra hours of sleep
→ One extra serving of vegetables a day → 365 more servings

You don't need a perfect diet or a dramatic transformation. You need to show up most days.

Pick one small habit from this year's posts. Start tomorrow.
